atoms.title: Boltzmann distribution
atoms.summary: At thermal equilibrium, the probability of a state falls off exponentially with its energy.

depths.eli5: Imagine a system can sit in several 'states', each costing a different amount of energy (like rungs on a ladder). Nature mostly settles on the cheap, low-energy rungs — but heat gives it random jiggles that occasionally bump it up to the expensive ones. The hotter it is, the more often the costly rungs get visited. 'Temperature' here is literally a measure of how strong those random jiggles are.
depths.core: A system kept at a fixed temperature T (by contact with a large surroundings, called a 'heat bath' — anything that can soak up or supply heat without changing temperature, like the water around a cell) sits in a given state i with a probability that drops off exponentially with that state's energy E_i. The recipe is the Boltzmann factor e^(−E_i/k_BT): double the energy gap and the state becomes far rarer. Here k_B is the Boltzmann constant (a fixed conversion factor between temperature and energy) and the product k_BT is an energy. This one rule underlies nearly every equilibrium argument in biophysics — protein folding, molecules binding to each other, and transport all reduce to comparing Boltzmann factors. 'Equilibrium' means the system has settled so its average behavior no longer changes with time.
depths.deep: k_BT (≈0.6 kcal/mol at body temperature, 310 K) is the natural energy scale of biology — the typical size of a thermal jiggle. A 'kcal/mol' is just a chemist's unit of energy per mole of molecules. Energy differences of only a few k_BT are the difference between 'almost always' and 'almost never', which is why biology operates on such small energy margins.

atoms.note: Memorize k_BT ≈ 0.6 kcal/mol ≈ 2.5 kJ/mol at 310 K (body temperature) — your unit of biological 'is this significant?'. If an energy difference is much bigger than k_BT it dominates; if much smaller, thermal noise washes it out.

atoms.title: Partition function
atoms.summary: The sum of all Boltzmann factors — the normalizer that turns energies into probabilities and free energies.

depths.eli5: Take every possible state the system could be in and add up how 'available' each one is (its Boltzmann factor — bigger for cheap, low-energy states). That single grand total, called Z, secretly contains everything you could measure about the system. It is also the number you divide by to turn raw 'availabilities' into real probabilities that add up to 100%.
depths.core: The partition function Z is the sum of the Boltzmann factors over every accessible state (a 'state' here means one specific microscopic arrangement, called a microstate). Z does two jobs: it normalizes the Boltzmann distribution (dividing by Z makes the probabilities sum to 1, the job of a normalizing constant), and it is the bridge to thermodynamics — once you can write Z, you can extract free energy, average energy, and any measurable quantity by taking derivatives of it. The letter Z comes from the German 'Zustandssumme', literally 'sum over states'.
depths.deep: For subsystems that don't interact, Z factorizes (Z = ∏ z_k, a product of the smaller partition functions). That is why two-state models and binding polynomials are so tractable: you multiply small, easy partition functions instead of summing over an astronomically large list of joint states.

quiz.answer: p_i = e^(−E_i/kT)/Z; Z is the normalization constant ensuring the probabilities sum to 1.

atoms.title: Free energy from the partition function
atoms.summary: Free energy is just the log of the partition function — the quantity systems minimize at constant T.

depths.eli5: Nature is pulled two ways: toward low energy (settling down) and toward 'many ways to be arranged' (spreading out, which is what entropy counts). Free energy is one number that balances those two urges. A system rolls until that number is as small as possible, and that resting point is equilibrium.
depths.core: The Helmholtz free energy F = −k_BT·ln Z (where ln is the natural logarithm and Z is the partition function) packages energy and entropy into a single quantity. At constant temperature and volume, a system reaches equilibrium at the state of minimum F, and any drop in F drives a spontaneous process — one that happens on its own without added energy. Entropy, the term doing battle with energy here, is essentially a count of how many microscopic arrangements correspond to a given overall state.
depths.deep: Equivalently F = U − TS, where U is the internal energy (the total energy stored in the system) and S is the entropy. The entropy term TS is why warm, floppy, high-multiplicity states can win even at a modest energy cost — it is the engine behind the hydrophobic effect and the springiness of disordered chains.

atoms.title: Gibbs free energy
atoms.summary: At constant temperature and pressure (the cell's condition), spontaneity is governed by ΔG.

depths.eli5: Will a change happen all by itself? Weigh two things against each other: how much heat the change gives off (good) versus how much orderliness it destroys (also tends to happen on its own). ΔG is the single scorecard. If ΔG is negative, the change is downhill and goes on its own; if positive, you have to push energy in to make it happen. The little triangle Δ just means 'the change in'.
depths.core: A living cell operates at roughly constant temperature and pressure, so the right energy bookkeeper is the Gibbs free energy G, not the Helmholtz F (which assumes constant volume). The change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines enthalpy H (the heat content — bonds made and broken, contacts formed) with entropy S (disorder, the count of arrangements), weighted by temperature T. Every binding strength and every folding equilibrium is really a ΔG in disguise.
depths.deep: The workhorse link is ΔG° = −RT·ln K, tying the standard free-energy change to the equilibrium constant K (the ratio of products to reactants once a reaction has settled). R is the gas constant (essentially Boltzmann's constant per mole). This is the equation you use to convert any measured binding constant K_d or equilibrium constant K_eq into an energy in kcal/mol.

atoms.note: ΔG°' = −RT·ln K — arguably the most-used equation in all of biochemistry (the prime ' marks the biochemical standard state at pH 7). It is how a measured ratio of bound-to-unbound becomes an energy.

atoms.title: Eigenvalues & normal modes
atoms.summary: Linear systems decompose into independent modes — directions that simply scale. This is how we read out collective motion.

depths.eli5: When a complicated object wobbles, the messy motion is really just a few simple wobbles happening at once, stacked on top of each other. If you can find those few simple, pure wobbles (called the normal modes), the whole confusing dance suddenly makes sense. The soft, easy wobbles are usually the ones that matter for what the object does.
depths.core: A matrix is just a grid of numbers that transforms vectors (a vector being a list of numbers, like a direction in space). An eigenvector of a matrix is a special direction that the matrix only stretches or shrinks — never rotates — and the eigenvalue is the amount of that stretch. For a protein modeled as connected springs, the relevant matrix encodes its stiffness; its eigenvectors are the normal modes (whole-molecule coordinated motions), and the smallest eigenvalues mark the soft, easily-excited, large-scale motions that tend to be biologically important.
depths.deep: Diagonalizing a matrix (rewriting it in terms of its eigenvectors) turns a tangle of coupled motions into a set of independent, simple oscillators. For molecules the relevant matrix is the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives of the energy) or, in simplified network models, a connectivity matrix. The low-frequency (soft) modes usually dominate functional conformational change.

atoms.title: The hydrophobic effect
atoms.summary: Nonpolar groups cluster in water not because they attract each other, but because water gains entropy when they hide.

depths.eli5: Oil drops in water clump together — not because the oil bits attract each other, but because the water wants them out of the way. Water molecules normally hold hands in a loose network; an oily ('nonpolar', meaning it can't hold hands with water) blob forces the nearby water into a stiff, orderly cage around it. Water hates being caged. So if you shove all the oily blobs together, less water has to form cages, and the freed water gets to be messy and happy again. The push comes from the water, not the oil.
depths.core: 'Nonpolar' groups are parts of a molecule with no electric charge imbalance, so they can't form hydrogen bonds with water. When such a group sits in water, the surrounding water molecules arrange into a relatively ordered 'cage'. Burying that nonpolar surface (hiding it inside a protein or membrane) releases the cage water back into the disordered bulk, which raises entropy — the count of available arrangements. So the driving force is largely entropic (a positive ΔS), which is why, oddly, the effect gets stronger as temperature rises over a wide range. This is the dominant force that folds proteins and assembles cell membranes.
depths.deep: The classic experimental fingerprint is a large positive heat-capacity change (ΔCp — how much the heat needed to warm the system changes) when nonpolar surface is exposed to water. A protein's net folding free energy is a small difference between large opposing enthalpy and entropy terms, leaving proteins only marginally stable (~5–15 kcal/mol, just a handful of k_BT).

atoms.note: Marginal stability (only a few k_BT of net stability) is a feature, not a bug: it lets proteins fold reversibly, be switched on and off, and be recycled when worn out.

atoms.title: Electrostatic screening & the Debye length
atoms.summary: Salt ions cloud around charges and cut off electrostatic interactions beyond the Debye length.

depths.eli5: Put an electric charge in salty water and the dissolved salt ions of the opposite sign swarm around it, forming a cloud that hides it. From a little distance away you barely 'feel' the original charge at all — the cloud cancels it out. The Debye length is roughly how far you have to be before that cloaking takes over.
depths.core: Salt dissolves into mobile ions (charged atoms), and they screen (electrically hide) any fixed charge: the electric potential — the strength of the charge's electrical influence — falls off as e^(−r/λ_D), where r is distance and λ_D is the Debye length. At the salt level inside a cell (about 150 millimolar, mM) λ_D ≈ 0.8 nanometers (nm, billionths of a meter), so electric forces inside cells reach only very short distances. This comes from the 'linearized' (small-charge approximation) version of the Poisson–Boltzmann equation.
depths.deep: λ_D shrinks in proportion to 1/√(ionic strength), where ionic strength is a measure of total dissolved-salt concentration weighted by ion charge. Experiments that gradually change the salt concentration are effectively dialing how far charges 'see' each other, which lets researchers measure the electrostatic contribution to binding and folding.

atoms.note: Rule of thumb: λ_D ≈ 0.3 nm / √(ionic strength in molar). At 0.1 M salt it's about 1 nm — roughly the width of a few water molecules.

atoms.title: Protein structure hierarchy
atoms.summary: Sequence (primary) → local helices/sheets (secondary) → 3D fold (tertiary) → assemblies (quaternary).

depths.eli5: A protein starts as a long string of beads (the beads are amino acids, the chemical building blocks). Stretches of that string first curl into simple local shapes — a spiral (helix) or a flat pleated ribbon (sheet). The whole string then folds up into one compact blob. Sometimes several blobs clip together into a bigger machine. Four levels: the bead order, the local shapes, the folded blob, and the team of blobs.
depths.core: Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence — the exact order of the ~20 building-block amino acids along the chain. Secondary structure is local repeating shapes of the backbone (the α-helix, a coil, and the β-sheet, a pleated ribbon), held together by hydrogen bonds (weak attractions between an H on one part and an O or N on another). Tertiary structure is the complete 3D fold of one chain. Quaternary structure is several folded chains assembled together. A protein's job is usually carried out at the tertiary and quaternary levels.
depths.deep: The α-helix and β-sheet were predicted on paper from hydrogen-bonding geometry (by Pauling and colleagues) before anyone saw them in a real structure — a landmark of pure structural reasoning. The shape of the backbone is captured by two rotation angles per residue, φ (phi) and ψ (psi), the dihedral (twist) angles that the Ramachandran plot maps out.

atoms.title: The Ramachandran plot
atoms.summary: Allowed backbone (φ, ψ) angles cluster into a few regions — and those regions ARE the secondary-structure types.

depths.eli5: Each link in a protein's backbone can twist in two places. But most twist combinations make atoms crash into each other, which isn't allowed. Plot the few combinations that DON'T crash and you get a couple of neat clusters — and those clusters are exactly the helix and sheet shapes proteins actually use. The rules of 'no bumping' alone explain the shapes.
depths.core: Atoms take up space and can't overlap; this 'steric' restriction (a steric clash is two atoms trying to occupy the same spot) limits the two backbone twist angles φ and ψ to just a few allowed regions. The α-helix and β-sheet land in separate clusters ('basins') on the φ–ψ plot. The plot is the standard quality-check for experimental structures: a residue sitting in a forbidden region usually signals an error.
depths.deep: Glycine, whose side chain is just a hydrogen atom, is small enough to access extra regions; proline, whose side chain loops back onto the backbone, is extra-restricted. The whole plot is a direct geometric consequence of excluded volume (atoms can't overlap) — a clean example of biological structure emerging from simple sterics.

atoms.title: The ideal polymer chain
atoms.summary: A flexible chain of N random links behaves like a random walk: its size grows as the square root of length.

depths.eli5: Picture a floppy string thrown down in random kinks, like a tangled phone cord. The two ends usually end up surprisingly close — the string doesn't reach far. And it scales weirdly: make the string 4 times longer and the tangle only gets about 2 times wider, because the kinks keep doubling back on themselves. This is the same math as a 'random walk', a stumble where each step points a random way.
depths.core: Model the chain as N segments, each of length b, where every segment points in a random direction independent of the others — exactly a random walk in 3D. The result is a loose ball (a 'Gaussian coil') whose end-to-end size R grows like b√N, i.e. as the square root of length, not linearly. This is the baseline 'no interactions at all' model for an unfolded protein or a stretch of DNA, and the yardstick against which real chains are compared.
depths.deep: If the chain can't pass through itself (excluded volume — real atoms take up space), the coil swells a bit more, to R ~ b·N^0.59 (Flory's result). A 'poor solvent' (one the chain dislikes being surrounded by) instead makes it collapse into a compact ball. Protein folding is, in part, a dramatic departure from these random-coil statistics toward one specific compact shape.

quiz.prompt: How does an ideal chain's size scale with the number of segments N?
quiz.answer: As √N (R ~ b√N) — like a random walk.

quiz.prompt: Why does ⟨R²⟩ = Nb² for independent segments? Sketch the reasoning.

atoms.title: Worm-like chain & persistence length
atoms.summary: Stiff polymers (like DNA) are characterized by a persistence length — the distance over which the chain 'forgets' its direction.

depths.eli5: Not all floppy strings are equally floppy. A piece of cooked spaghetti stays straight for a stretch before it droops; a wet noodle bends right away. The 'persistence length' is how far along the string it stays pointing roughly the same way before it forgets its direction. Short pieces (shorter than that length) act like stiff rods; long pieces act like tangled coils.
depths.core: The worm-like chain (WLC) model describes 'semiflexible' polymers — chains that are neither perfectly stiff nor perfectly floppy, but have some bending stiffness. The persistence length l_p is the key number: it marks the changeover from rod-like behavior (for pieces shorter than l_p) to coil-like behavior (for pieces much longer than l_p). DNA is quite stiff, with l_p ≈ 50 nm; a disordered (unstructured) protein is very floppy, l_p ≈ 0.5–1 nm.
depths.deep: The WLC's force-versus-extension relationship — how hard you must pull to stretch it to a given length — is what single-molecule pulling experiments (optical and magnetic tweezers) fit to. That lets researchers measure the mechanical properties of one individual DNA or protein molecule at a time.

atoms.title: Two-state folding equilibrium
atoms.summary: Many small proteins fold all-or-none: only folded and unfolded states are populated, set by a single ΔG.

depths.eli5: Lots of small proteins behave like a light switch: they're either fully ON (folded into their working shape) or fully OFF (unfolded into a floppy string), with almost nothing caught half-way. Heat them up or add a chemical that unfolds proteins, and they flip from mostly-folded to mostly-unfolded over a surprisingly narrow range.
depths.core: The two-state approximation says only two states matter — folded (F) and unfolded (U) — and the balance between them is set by a single free-energy difference, ΔG_fold. The experimental tell is a cooperative, S-shaped ('sigmoidal') melting curve: as you raise temperature or add a 'denaturant' (an unfolding chemical like urea), the fraction folded drops sharply rather than gradually. Fitting that curve gives you ΔG. 'Cooperative' means the parts fold or unfold together, all-or-none, rather than independently.
depths.deep: Why all-or-none? Partially-folded states sit higher in free energy than either fully-folded or fully-unfolded — the folding 'funnel' makes the in-between region unfavorable. So the population piles up at the two ends (it is bimodal), and the molecule spends almost no time in between.

quiz.answer: A cooperative, sigmoidal transition (vs temperature or denaturant) with only folded and unfolded states populated.

atoms.title: Energy landscape & the folding funnel
atoms.summary: Folding is a biased downhill search on a funnel-shaped landscape, not a single pathway.

depths.eli5: Imagine a ball rolling down the inside of a funnel toward the spout. There are countless paths down, but they all end at the same bottom point. A protein folds the same way: it starts as one of a huge number of floppy shapes near the wide rim and tumbles 'downhill' (toward lower energy) until it reaches its one finished shape at the bottom. Many routes, one destination.
depths.core: The old picture imagined a single fixed folding route. Energy-landscape theory replaced it with a statistical funnel: a vast number of high-energy unfolded shapes near the top, narrowing toward the single low-energy 'native' (working) shape at the bottom. The funnel's downhill slope (an energetic bias toward more-folded shapes) outcompetes the enormous number of possible shapes, which solves Levinthal's paradox — the puzzle that a protein could never fold in a reasonable time if it had to try every shape at random.
depths.deep: Real funnels are 'rugged' — dotted with small dips (local minima) that can briefly trap a half-folded molecule or send it down the wrong path (misfolding). The 'principle of minimal frustration' says evolution has tuned protein sequences so their funnels are smooth enough to fold reliably despite this ruggedness.

atoms.title: Anfinsen's thermodynamic hypothesis
atoms.summary: The native structure is encoded by the sequence alone — it is the global free-energy minimum.

depths.eli5: All the information a protein needs to find its shape is already baked into its bead-order (its sequence). Anfinsen proved it: he unraveled an enzyme into a floppy string, removed the chemicals holding it open, and it spontaneously folded right back into its exact working shape — no instructions needed. The shape is the sequence's destiny.
depths.core: Anfinsen showed that a 'denatured' (unfolded) enzyme can refold on its own into its active form once normal conditions are restored. The implication: the native (working) structure is the most thermodynamically stable shape for that amino-acid sequence under physiological conditions — i.e. the global minimum of free energy. This is the founding principle of structure prediction: if shape follows from sequence, then in principle you can compute shape from sequence.
depths.deep: Caveats from inside living cells: 'chaperone' proteins help others fold faster (assisting the kinetics, the speed, not the final answer); some proteins get kinetically trapped in a wrong shape, or must fold while still being made (co-translational folding). Still, the thermodynamic hypothesis remains the conceptual bedrock of the field — and the premise behind modern predictors like AlphaFold.

atoms.title: Mutational stability change (ΔΔG)
atoms.summary: How much a point mutation stabilizes or destabilizes the fold — the workhorse number of protein engineering.

depths.eli5: Swap out just one of a protein's amino-acid beads for a different one. Does the protein now hold its shape better or worse than before? That change-in-the-change is called ΔΔG. ('Wild type' just means the normal, unmutated version; a 'mutant' is the changed one.)
depths.core: ΔΔG compares the folding free energy ΔG of a mutant to that of the wild type (the original). It is a 'change of a change' — hence the double delta. With the common convention, a positive ΔΔG means the mutation destabilizes (weakens) the fold. Predicting ΔΔG from a protein's structure is a central task in protein engineering and in judging whether a genetic variant is harmful — and a place where simple physics models often match or beat machine learning.
depths.deep: Folding stability is not the same observable as aggregation (clumping) or biochemical function. A mutation can stabilize the fold yet still cause disease — for instance by making the protein clump. So the lesson is to match the measured quantity to the actual question being asked.

atoms.note: Sign conventions differ between software tools — always check which direction their 'destabilizing' points before trusting a number.

quiz.answer: Yes — stability and aggregation/function are different observables; a mutation can stabilize the fold yet promote aggregation or impair function.

atoms.title: Binding & the dissociation constant
atoms.summary: K_d is the ligand concentration at which a site is half-occupied — the universal currency of molecular recognition.

depths.eli5: A 'ligand' is just any small molecule that sticks to a protein (a drug, a hormone, oxygen). Slowly add more and more ligand to a pot of protein. The K_d is the ligand concentration at which exactly half the protein molecules have something stuck to them. A small K_d means you only needed a tiny amount of ligand to reach half — so it sticks tightly. Big K_d, weak sticking.
depths.core: From the law of mass action (the rule that reaction rates depend on how much of each ingredient is present), the fraction of sites occupied, θ, follows a hyperbola: θ = [L]/(K_d + [L]), where [L] is free-ligand concentration. Plug in [L] = K_d and you get θ = 0.5 — half occupied. K_d converts directly to an energy via ΔG° = RT·ln K_d, so a binder 10 times tighter is about 1.4 kcal/mol more stable. K_d is the universal currency for how strongly two molecules recognize each other.
depths.deep: K_d also equals k_off/k_on — the ratio of the 'off' rate (how fast bound ligand falls off) to the 'on' rate (how fast it attaches). This ties the equilibrium (K_d) to the kinetics (the rates). Many drugs are actually optimized on a slow k_off — long 'residence time' on the target — rather than on K_d alone.

atoms.note: Rough scale: nanomolar (nM) K_d ≈ tight binding, micromolar (µM) ≈ moderate, millimolar (mM) ≈ weak. Every 10× change in K_d ≈ 1.4 kcal/mol at body temperature (310 K).

atoms.title: Cooperativity & the Hill equation
atoms.summary: When binding one ligand helps the next, the binding curve sharpens from a hyperbola into a switch.

depths.eli5: Some proteins have several binding spots. If grabbing the first ligand makes the protein hungrier for the next one, then once binding starts it quickly snowballs. The result is a sharp switch: almost nothing bound, then suddenly almost everything bound, over a narrow range of concentration — instead of the gentle, gradual curve you'd get from independent spots.
depths.core: The Hill coefficient n is a single number summarizing cooperativity. n = 1 means the sites act independently (ordinary hyperbola, no teamwork); n > 1 means positive cooperativity — binding one ligand boosts the affinity for the next — giving an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve. Hemoglobin binding oxygen (n ≈ 2.8 across its four sites) is the classic example, and it's what makes oxygen pickup and delivery efficient.
depths.deep: The Hill equation is 'phenomenological' — a useful curve-fit rather than a mechanism. The theoretical maximum n equals the number of sites (perfect all-or-none binding). To explain WHERE cooperativity actually comes from, you need mechanistic models like MWC (concerted) and KNF (sequential).

quiz.answer: Positive cooperativity — binding one ligand increases affinity for the next, giving a sigmoidal (switch-like) curve.

quiz.prompt: Why is cooperative O₂ binding useful for hemoglobin?
quiz.answer: The sigmoidal curve lets it load O₂ in the lungs and unload it in tissues over a small change in O₂ pressure.

atoms.title: MWC allostery
atoms.summary: Cooperativity from a concerted switch between a tense (T) and relaxed (R) state of the whole assembly.

depths.eli5: Picture a protein made of identical pieces that always flip shape together, all at once, between a 'tense' shape (bad at grabbing ligand) and a 'relaxed' shape (good at grabbing ligand). Both shapes are always present in some mix. When ligand is around it sticks better to the relaxed shape, so it tips the whole crowd toward relaxed — and that tipping is where the cooperative, switch-like behavior comes from.
depths.core: The Monod–Wyman–Changeux (MWC) model: an 'oligomer' (a protein built from several identical subunits) already exists in two interconverting states — T (tense, low ligand affinity) and R (relaxed, high affinity) — in equilibrium, even before any ligand arrives. Because ligand binds the R state better, binding shifts the population toward R. This 'concerted' (all-subunits-together) switch produces cooperativity without any 'induced fit', where binding would reshape one site at a time.
depths.deep: MWC (concerted) and KNF (sequential) are the two classic frameworks for allostery (regulation at a distance). Real proteins often fall between them. MWC's idea that ligand simply selects a pre-existing shape — 'conformational selection' — connects directly to modern ensemble and energy-landscape thinking.

quiz.prompt: In MWC, where does cooperativity come from?
quiz.answer: From a pre-existing equilibrium between a low-affinity (T) and high-affinity (R) state; ligand binding shifts the whole assembly toward R.

quiz.prompt: How does MWC differ from the KNF (induced-fit) model?
quiz.answer: MWC is concerted (all subunits switch together, conformational selection); KNF is sequential (each binding event induces a local change).

atoms.title: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
atoms.summary: Enzyme rate rises with substrate then saturates; K_M and V_max characterize the enzyme.

depths.eli5: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction, and the 'substrate' is the stuff it works on. Feed an enzyme more substrate and it works faster — but only up to a point. Once every enzyme molecule is busy all the time, piling on more substrate can't help; it's already going flat out. The speed levels off at a ceiling.
depths.core: Assuming the amount of enzyme–substrate complex holds roughly steady (the steady-state, or Briggs–Haldane, assumption), the starting reaction rate v traces a hyperbola as substrate [S] increases. K_M (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half the maximum rate, V_max — loosely a measure of how readily the enzyme grabs substrate. The ratio k_cat/K_M (k_cat being the top turnover speed per enzyme) is the 'specificity constant' used to compare how good different enzymes are.
depths.deep: k_cat/K_M can't exceed the speed at which enzyme and substrate find each other by diffusion (~10^8–10^9 per molar per second). Enzymes that hit this ceiling are called 'catalytically perfect' — directly linking enzyme kinetics back to the physics of diffusion.

atoms.title: Transition-state theory (Eyring)
atoms.summary: Reaction rate is set by the free-energy barrier to a transition state — the bridge from thermodynamics to kinetics.

depths.eli5: Between the starting molecules and the finished product there's an energy 'hill' to climb. The reaction can only happen as fast as it's easy to get over that hill. A tall hill means the reaction crawls; a low hill means it races. The very top of the hill — the most awkward, halfway-rearranged moment — is the 'transition state'.
depths.core: Eyring's equation relates a reaction's rate constant to the activation free energy ΔG‡ — the height of the energy barrier up to the transition state (the ‡ symbol marks 'of the transition state'). The leading factor k_BT/h (about 6×10^12 per second at body temperature, where h is Planck's constant) sets the basic 'attempt frequency'. This explains two things at once: catalysis means lowering the barrier, and reaction rates are extremely sensitive to temperature.
depths.deep: An enzyme speeds a reaction by binding the awkward transition state more tightly than it binds the comfortable starting substrate — Linus Pauling's insight. That is also the rationale for 'transition-state-analog' drugs: molecules shaped like the transition state jam the enzyme by binding where it grips hardest.

atoms.title: Diffusion — Fick's laws
atoms.summary: Matter flows down concentration gradients; the diffusion coefficient D sets how fast.

depths.eli5: Drop a bit of dye in still water and it slowly spreads out from where it's crowded toward where there's none — no stirring needed. Fick's law just says: the steeper the difference in crowding from one spot to the next (the 'gradient'), the faster stuff flows to even it out. 'Flux' is simply the amount of stuff crossing an area each second.
depths.core: Fick's first law says the diffusive flux J (how much material crosses a unit area per second) is proportional to the concentration gradient ∇c (how sharply concentration changes with position), pointing from high to low. Combine it with conservation of matter (nothing vanishes) and you get the diffusion equation, ∂c/∂t = D∇²c, which predicts how a concentration evolves over time. The diffusion coefficient D measures how fast a given molecule spreads. Diffusion is how molecules find their targets inside cells and it sets the speed limit of any transport that isn't actively stirred.
depths.deep: Diffusion is the large-scale face of random molecular jiggling. The very same D shows up in the microscopic mean-square-displacement law (see random walk) and in the Einstein relation that ties it to temperature and friction.

atoms.title: Einstein–Stokes relation
atoms.summary: Diffusion, temperature, viscosity, and size are linked — bigger and stickier means slower.

depths.eli5: How fast a tiny particle wanders around in a liquid depends on four things: how warm it is (warmer = more jiggle), how thick the liquid is (honey vs water), and how big the particle is. Small things in thin, warm liquid zip around; big things in thick, cold liquid barely crawl. This formula ties all of that together.
depths.core: The Einstein relation D = k_BT/γ says the diffusion coefficient D equals the thermal energy k_BT divided by the friction (drag) coefficient γ. For a sphere of radius r moving through a liquid of viscosity η (its 'thickness' or resistance to flow), Stokes' law gives γ = 6πηr. Put them together: D = k_BT/(6πηr). This lets you estimate how fast a molecule diffuses from its size, or work out its size from a measured D (as in dynamic light scattering).
depths.deep: This is a 'fluctuation–dissipation' result: the very same friction γ that slows a particle down (dissipation) also sets the strength of the random thermal kicks that keep it moving (fluctuation). Drag and noise are two faces of one coin — you can't have one without the other at a given temperature.

atoms.title: Random walk & mean-square displacement
atoms.summary: Diffusing molecules spread as the square root of time — the microscopic origin of Fick's laws.

depths.eli5: Imagine someone stumbling, each step in a random direction. They drift away from the start, but very inefficiently: to end up twice as far away takes four times as many steps. 'Mean-square displacement' is just the typical squared distance from the start — a fair way to measure spread when the average direction is zero.
depths.core: For unbiased random motion (no preferred direction), the mean-square displacement grows in direct proportion to time: ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt in one dimension (6Dt in three). The typical distance traveled is therefore the square root of that, ∝ √t. This √t scaling is exactly why diffusion is lightning-fast across a few nanometers but hopelessly slow across centimeters — and it's the reason cells that rely on diffusion to feed themselves can't be very large. This random-walk picture is the microscopic origin of Fick's laws.
depths.deep: When ⟨x²⟩ instead grows as t^α with α ≠ 1, you have 'anomalous diffusion': α < 1 (subdiffusion) signals molecular crowding or sticky binding, α > 1 (superdiffusion) signals active transport. Watching single particles inside living cells and measuring α is a rich readout of the crowded cellular interior.

atoms.note: Diffusion time scales as L²/D (distance squared over the diffusion coefficient) — always estimate it before assuming transport across some distance is 'fast'.

atoms.title: The Nernst potential
atoms.summary: The membrane voltage at which an ion's concentration gradient is exactly balanced by the electric field.

depths.eli5: An ion is a charged atom (like sodium or potassium). It naturally wants to drift from where it's crowded to where it's sparse. But because it carries charge, if it piles up on one side it builds a voltage that pushes back. Crank that voltage up to just the right value and the push from crowding exactly cancels the electrical push-back — so on average the ion stops flowing. That exact balancing voltage is the Nernst potential.
depths.core: For an ion the membrane lets through (a 'permeant' ion), there are two forces: a chemical one (from the concentration difference inside vs outside) and an electrical one (from the voltage across the membrane). At the Nernst (equilibrium) potential these two exactly cancel and there's no net flow. Each ion has its own Nernst potential — the 'target' voltage it tries to drag the membrane toward — and these are the foundation of cellular electrophysiology (the study of electrical signals in cells).
depths.deep: When several ions can cross at once, you blend their Nernst potentials weighted by how easily each crosses (its 'permeability') using the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation to get the cell's resting voltage. But each individual ion's Nernst potential remains the reference point it pulls toward.

atoms.note: At body temperature (310 K), the factor (RT/F)·ln works out to about 61 mV per tenfold (one 'decade') change in concentration ratio, divided by the ion's charge z.

atoms.title: Lipid bilayer self-assembly
atoms.summary: Amphiphilic lipids spontaneously form bilayers — the cell's barrier — driven by the hydrophobic effect.

depths.eli5: Lipids are soap-like molecules: one end loves water (the 'head'), the other end is oily and hates water (the 'tails'). Drop a lot of them in water and they spontaneously line up — heads facing out toward the water on both surfaces, oily tails hiding in the middle pointing at each other. The result is a thin double sheet that water can't easily cross: the skin of every cell.
depths.core: Because each lipid has a water-loving (polar) head and water-hating (nonpolar) tails, hiding the tails away from water (the hydrophobic effect) drives them to assemble, all by themselves, into a two-layer sheet — a bilayer. 'Amphiphilic' means having both water-loving and water-hating parts. The sheet is fluid (lipids slide around within it) and self-healing, and it is the structural basis of all cell membranes and of dividing the cell into compartments.
depths.deep: A lipid's overall shape (summarized by its 'packing parameter') decides whether it forms a flat bilayer, a ball-shaped micelle, or other phases. How much energy it costs to bend or fuse a bilayer (see Helfrich elasticity) governs vesicles (tiny membrane bubbles), membrane shaping, and the formation of pores.

atoms.title: Hodgkin–Huxley & the action potential
atoms.summary: Voltage-gated ion conductances make the membrane an excitable circuit that fires all-or-none spikes.

depths.eli5: A nerve cell's surface is dotted with tiny gates that open and close depending on the voltage across the membrane. When voltage rises past a threshold, sodium gates fling open and the voltage spikes upward; then potassium gates open and bring it back down. That fast up-then-down pulse is a nerve 'spike', and chains of these spikes are how neurons talk.
depths.core: Treat the membrane as an electrical circuit: a capacitor (it stores charge) wired in parallel with several ion-specific 'conductances' (how easily each ion flows). Hodgkin and Huxley wrote equations showing how voltage-dependent sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) conductances — controlled by 'gating variables' that track how open the gates are — generate the action potential: a fast Na⁺ inflow drives the voltage up (depolarization), then a slower K⁺ outflow brings it back down (repolarization). Each ion current pushes the voltage toward that ion's Nernst potential.
depths.deep: This was a quantitative, predictive model fit to careful voltage-clamp measurements (a technique that holds the voltage fixed and reads the resulting current) — a landmark of biophysics. Remarkably, the abstract gating variables foreshadowed the real molecular machinery of voltage-gated ion channels discovered decades later.

atoms.title: Elastic network models (GNM/ENM)
atoms.summary: Model a protein as nodes connected by springs; the soft normal modes predict functional flexibility remarkably well.

depths.eli5: Forget all the chemistry: just pretend a protein is a bunch of balls (one per amino acid) joined by springs wherever two balls sit close together. Now ask where this toy springs-and-balls model naturally wobbles most. Astonishingly, those wobbly spots match the floppy parts of the real protein. Shape and connectivity, not chemical detail, carry most of the flexibility information.
depths.core: The Gaussian Network Model (GNM) connects any two residues closer than a cutoff distance with identical springs, then finds the natural vibration modes by diagonalizing the network's connectivity matrix (the Kirchhoff matrix — a table of which nodes are linked). Despite ignoring all chemical specifics, its low-frequency (soft) modes reproduce experimental flexibility measures like crystallographic B-factors and simulation RMSF (root-mean-square fluctuation — how much each atom jiggles). The takeaway: flexibility is largely set by which residues contact which (the 'contact topology'), not by chemistry.
depths.deep: Because GNM has essentially no free parameters and is computed analytically (from a formula, not trained on data), it cannot secretly exploit similarity to known proteins ('homology leakage'). That makes it a strong, honest baseline that any machine-learning flexibility predictor must genuinely beat to prove it learned real physics.

atoms.note: A recurring lesson in this corpus: simple physics baselines (like GNM) often match or beat machine learning for predicting flexibility.

atoms.title: Molecular dynamics
atoms.summary: Integrate Newton's equations on a force field to watch biomolecules move atom-by-atom.

depths.eli5: Molecular dynamics is like a physics video game for atoms. At each instant, the computer works out the force on every atom from its neighbors, nudges each one a tiny step accordingly, and then repeats — millions or billions of times. String the frames together and you get a movie of the molecule wiggling and rearranging, atom by atom.
depths.core: MD numerically solves Newton's law of motion, F = ma (force equals mass times acceleration), one tiny timestep at a time, using a clever stepping recipe called the Verlet algorithm. The forces come from an empirical 'force field' — a set of simple rules for the energy of stretched bonds, bent angles, electrostatic attraction/repulsion, and weak van der Waals contacts. The output is a trajectory (a movie) from which thermodynamic and kinetic properties are computed, connecting structure to function in motion.
depths.deep: The central headache is sampling: simulation steps are femtoseconds (10^-15 s) but biologically interesting events can take milliseconds — a billion-billion-fold gap. To reach rare events you need 'enhanced sampling' tricks (umbrella sampling, metadynamics) or Markov state models that stitch many short simulations into the slow picture.

atoms.title: AlphaFold & pLDDT
atoms.summary: Deep learning predicts structure from sequence; pLDDT is its per-residue confidence — often misread as flexibility.

depths.eli5: AlphaFold is an AI that reads a protein's sequence of letters (its amino acids) and guesses the 3D shape it folds into. At each spot it also prints a number saying how confident it is. The trap: people see a low-confidence spot and assume that part of the protein is floppy. But 'the AI is unsure here' is not the same as 'this part actually wiggles'.
depths.core: AlphaFold predicts a protein's 3D structure from its sequence plus a 'multiple-sequence alignment' (a stack of related proteins from other species, which reveals which positions evolved together). It reports pLDDT, a per-residue confidence score from 0 to 100. On average, low-pLDDT regions do tend to be disordered or flexible — but pLDDT is a measure of prediction confidence, not a physical measurement of motion. Whether it can stand in for flexibility was an active 2025 debate.
depths.deep: Treating pLDDT as if it were dynamics is a classic 'observable-mismatch' and data-leakage trap: confidence partly reflects how predictable (e.g. how evolutionarily conserved) a region is, not how much it moves. So an honest flexibility benchmark must compare against an actual physics model (like GNM) and carefully control for homology (similarity to training proteins).

atoms.title: Protein language models (ESM)
atoms.summary: Transformers trained on millions of sequences learn representations that predict structure, function, and mutation effects.

depths.eli5: Treat each protein as a sentence written in a 20-letter alphabet (the amino acids). Show an AI millions of these 'sentences' and have it play fill-in-the-blank — hide a letter and make it guess. To win the game it has to learn the hidden grammar of proteins, which turns out to be enough to predict structure and to estimate what happens when you change a letter.
depths.core: Just like a text language model, ESM (Evolutionary Scale Modeling) is trained by 'masked-token prediction' — hide an amino acid and predict it — over huge databases of protein sequences (this is 'self-supervised' learning: the data labels itself). The model's internal representations ('embeddings') capture evolutionary and structural signal that's reusable for other tasks. But on some tasks, like predicting flexibility, sequence-only models can lose to simple physics and can secretly rely on similarity to training proteins.
depths.deep: To judge these models honestly you must test on proteins whose folds don't appear in training — e.g. splits that keep whole CATH superfamilies separate. Otherwise the apparent skill is partly memorized homology (recognizing near-copies of training data) rather than transferable biophysics.

atoms.note: A theme across modern biophysics ML: control for homology leakage (test on truly novel folds) or your benchmark will flatter the model and lie to you.

atoms.title: Disordered proteins & phase separation
atoms.summary: Many proteins lack a fixed fold; some demix into liquid droplets that organize the cell without membranes.

depths.eli5: Not every protein folds into a fixed shape — some stay floppy and shapeless on purpose. When lots of these floppy proteins are around and lightly stick to each other in many places, they can suddenly demix from the watery surroundings into liquid droplets, the way oil separates from water. These droplets act like little membraneless rooms that gather and sort the cell's contents.
depths.core: 'Intrinsically disordered' regions don't settle into one structure; they wander through a whole ensemble of shapes. When such regions make many weak, 'multivalent' contacts (multivalent = many sticky points per molecule), the mixture can undergo liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) — splitting into a dense droplet phase and a dilute surrounding phase. The droplets, called biomolecular condensates, compartmentalize biochemistry without needing a membrane.
depths.deep: The exact pattern of the sequence matters: blocks of charge and scattered aromatic 'sticker' residues tune whether and when droplets form. Worryingly, droplets can sometimes harden over time from liquid to solid, and that aberrant transition is linked to amyloid disease — directly connecting phase separation to protein aggregation.

atoms.title: Amyloid aggregation & nucleation
atoms.summary: Proteins can misassemble into ordered β-sheet fibrils through a nucleation-and-growth process central to neurodegeneration.

depths.eli5: Some proteins can mis-stick to each other and lock into long, highly ordered fibers (amyloid fibrils). The hard part is getting the very first little clump (the 'seed') to form — that's slow and rare. But once a seed exists, more protein piles onto its ends quickly, and the fiber grows. This seed-then-grow process is the hallmark of diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
depths.core: Amyloid formation follows nucleation–elongation kinetics: a slow, unfavorable 'nucleation' step forms a tiny seed, then 'elongation' adds molecules to the fibril ends, and fibrils can even spawn new seeds along their sides ('secondary nucleation'), accelerating the process. Crucially, a mutation's effect on disease often depends on its aggregation propensity (how sticky the sequence is) rather than on its effect on fold stability (ΔΔG).
depths.deep: A dye called Thioflavin-T lights up when it binds amyloid, so its fluorescence traces the characteristic S-shaped (sigmoidal) growth curve. For amyloid proteins that have no stable fold to begin with, a folding-stability predictor is simply the wrong tool — aggregation-propensity scales (like AGGRESCAN) match the actual disease behavior far better. A clean lesson in matching the method to the question.

atoms.note: Match the observable to the question: for disordered amyloid mutants, aggregation propensity (stickiness) beats folding stability (ΔΔG) as a predictor.

atoms.title: MD datasets at scale (mdCATH)
atoms.summary: Large, fold-diverse MD archives enable proteome-scale, leakage-controlled tests of biophysical hypotheses.

depths.eli5: It's easy to fool yourself studying just one protein — whatever you find might be a quirk of that one molecule. mdCATH is a giant library of computer simulations covering thousands of different protein shapes. With it, you can test an idea across the whole zoo of proteins and see if it really holds up, instead of trusting a single example.
depths.core: Datasets like mdCATH provide all-atom molecular-dynamics trajectories for thousands of protein domains (drawn from the CATH classification of fold types) at several temperatures. This lets you ask whether a proposed rule — say, which part unfolds first, or what predicts flexibility — holds across the full space of folds, tested under honest splits that keep related folds out of both training and testing. That turns one-off anecdotes into real benchmarks.
depths.deep: A recurring finding at scale: 'lore' learned from a single well-studied protein often fails to generalize, while simple structural and topological features (contact order, elastic network models) carry most of the transferable signal — a humbling but useful corrective to over-fitting to favorite examples.

quiz.answer: Proteome-scale, homology-controlled (fold-disjoint) tests of whether a biophysical rule generalizes across fold space.

quiz.answer: To prevent homology leakage, so measured skill reflects genuine generalization rather than memorized fold similarity.

atoms.title: Poisson–Boltzmann electrostatics
atoms.summary: The mean-field equation for the electrostatic potential around a charged molecule in salt water — Boltzmann-weighted mobile ions plugged into Poisson's equation.

depths.eli5: A charged protein pulls a cloud of opposite ions around itself. This equation tells you the shape of that cloud and how quickly the protein's pull fades with distance.
depths.core: Take Poisson's equation, ∇²φ = −ρ/(εε₀), and feed it a mobile-ion charge density set by the Boltzmann factor: each ion species sits at concentration nᵢ⁰·e^(−qᵢφ/kT). The result is a self-consistent, nonlinear PDE for the potential φ around a fixed charge distribution. Solve it (numerically, e.g. APBS) and you get binding electrostatics, pKa shifts, and salt dependence.
depths.deep: Linearizing the exponential for small φ collapses PB to Debye–Hückel, ∇²φ = κ²φ, where κ = 1/λ_D — so the Debye length is literally the decay constant of the linearized theory. PB is mean-field: it ignores ion–ion correlations, finite ion size, and dielectric saturation, which is why it fails for multivalent ions (Mg²⁺, polyamines) and highly charged nucleic acids.

atoms.note: PB is the workhorse behind continuum-electrostatics tools (APBS, DelPhi). Its failure modes (multivalent counterions, DNA) are exactly where ion correlations matter. ('Mean-field' means each ion feels the average cloud, not the jostling of individual neighbors.)

quiz.prompt: What two equations are combined to derive the Poisson–Boltzmann equation?
quiz.answer: Poisson's equation (∇²φ = −ρ/εε₀) and the Boltzmann distribution for the mobile-ion concentrations (nᵢ ∝ e^(−qᵢφ/kT)).

quiz.prompt: Show how the Debye length arises from PB.
quiz.answer: Expand the Boltzmann factor for small qφ/kT; the linear term gives ∇²φ = κ²φ with κ² = Σ nᵢ⁰qᵢ²/(εε₀kT). The decay length λ_D = 1/κ is the Debye length — the linearized (Debye–Hückel) limit of PB.

atoms.title: The Langevin equation
atoms.summary: Newton's law for a particle in a fluid: deterministic drag plus a random kicking force, with the two tied together by fluctuation–dissipation.

depths.eli5: A pollen grain in water gets dragged (slowed) by the fluid and randomly kicked by molecules hitting it. Write F = ma with both forces and you can predict how it wanders.
depths.core: m·dv/dt = −γv + ξ(t), where γ is Stokes drag and ξ(t) is a random force with zero mean. The kicks and the drag are not independent: ⟨ξ(t)ξ(t′)⟩ = 2γk_BT·δ(t−t′). This fluctuation–dissipation relation is what forces the particle to thermalize to k_BT, and it is why the same γ sets both the friction and the noise.
depths.deep: In the overdamped (high-friction) limit inertia drops out: γ·dx/dt = −∂U/∂x + ξ(t). Averaging recovers ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt with D = k_BT/γ (Einstein–Stokes). The Langevin picture in configuration space is dual to the Fokker–Planck/Smoluchowski equation for the probability density, and is the integrator behind Brownian and Langevin-dynamics MD.

atoms.note: Fluctuation–dissipation: the same γ (friction) that drains a particle's energy also injects the random kicks that keep it warm. Break that link in a simulation and it won't settle to the right temperature. ('Overdamped' = friction so strong that the particle's momentum is forgotten almost instantly, so only its position matters.)

atoms.title: Diffusion-limited rate (Smoluchowski)
atoms.summary: The fastest a bimolecular reaction can go when every diffusive encounter reacts — set purely by how quickly partners find each other.

depths.eli5: If two molecules react instantly the moment they touch, the only thing limiting the reaction is how fast they bump into each other by random wandering. This gives that speed limit.
depths.core: Solve the steady-state diffusion equation for partners approaching an absorbing sphere of radius R and you get k = 4πDR, where D is the relative diffusion coefficient (D = D_A + D_B). For typical proteins this ceiling is ~10⁹–10¹⁰ M⁻¹s⁻¹. A measured on-rate near this value means binding is diffusion-limited; far below it means an energy barrier or orientational/steric constraints gate the encounter.
depths.deep: Electrostatics rescales R by a Debye–Hückel factor (attraction speeds, like charges slow). Orientational constraints — only a small reactive patch counts — give the Berg–von Hippel reduction, partly rescued by reduction-in-dimensionality (sliding along DNA, membrane confinement). Enzymes like acetylcholinesterase and superoxide dismutase use electrostatic steering to beat the naive 4πDR estimate.

atoms.note: Diffusion-limited on-rates (~10⁹ per molar per second) are the speed limit when every touch reacts; faster apparent rates signal electrostatic steering or dimensional reduction (e.g. sliding along DNA), not magic. ('On-rate' = how fast two molecules first find and bind each other.)

quiz.answer: Binding is not purely diffusion-limited — an activation barrier, restrictive orientation, or steric gating slows reaction below the encounter rate.

atoms.title: Kramers escape over a barrier
atoms.summary: The rate a thermally-kicked particle escapes a potential well — Arrhenius exponential times a friction-dependent prefactor, the dynamical correction to transition-state theory.

depths.eli5: A ball jiggling in a valley occasionally gets enough random kicks to climb over a hill and escape. How often that happens depends on the hill's height and how 'sticky' the surrounding fluid is.
depths.core: Kramers solved the Langevin escape problem. The rate factors as k = A·e^(−ΔU/k_BT): the Boltzmann factor for the barrier height ΔU times a prefactor A set by the curvatures of the well and barrier and by the friction γ. In the high-friction (overdamped) limit, k = (ω₀ω_b)/(2πγ)·e^(−ΔU/k_BT) — crucially, the rate falls as 1/γ.
depths.deep: This exposes what transition-state theory misses: TST assumes every crossing of the barrier top is productive, but with friction the system can recross. The full Kramers result is non-monotonic in γ — the 'turnover': at low friction energy diffusion limits the rate (k ∝ γ), at high friction spatial diffusion does (k ∝ 1/γ). Protein folding and isomerization live in the high-friction regime, which is why solvent viscosity changes folding rates.

atoms.note: Kramers turnover: the escape rate rises then falls as friction increases (too little friction starves the climb of energy; too much friction bogs down the crossing). Transition-state theory (Eyring) is the zero-friction, no-recrossing idealization that Kramers corrects. ('Recrossing' = the system tops the barrier but slips back instead of reacting.)

atoms.title: X-ray diffraction & Bragg's law
atoms.summary: Crystals diffract X-rays into sharp spots where path differences between lattice planes are whole wavelengths — the original route to atomic-resolution structure.

depths.eli5: Line up molecules in a regular crystal, shine X-rays through, and they bounce off in special directions that make bright spots. The pattern of spots encodes where the atoms are.
depths.core: Constructive interference from parallel lattice planes spaced d apart requires nλ = 2d·sinθ (Bragg's law). The diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the electron density; spot positions give the unit cell, spot intensities give |F(hkl)|². Because detectors record intensity, the phases are lost — the phase problem — solved by molecular replacement, isomorphous replacement, or anomalous scattering.
depths.deep: Resolution is set by the highest-angle spots you can measure (smaller d ↔ larger θ). The map you build is the inverse FT of the structure factors F(hkl) = Σ f_j·e^(2πi(hx+ky+lz)); getting the phases right matters far more than the amplitudes ('phase dominance'). Crystal packing can distort flexible regions, and a static map averages over the crystal's molecules and time — a key contrast with NMR ensembles.

atoms.note: The 'phase problem' is the crux: a detector records how bright each spot is (the amplitude) but not its timing offset (the phase), and the phases carry most of the structural information. ('Diffraction' = waves bending and interfering after passing a regular array; a 'lattice plane' is one of the flat sheets of atoms in a crystal.)

quiz.prompt: Why is solving a crystal structure called the 'phase problem'?
quiz.answer: Detectors record intensities (∝ |F|²), giving structure-factor amplitudes but not their phases. The electron-density map is the inverse Fourier transform of F = |F|·e^(iφ), and the phases carry most of the structural information, so they must be recovered separately (molecular/isomorphous replacement, anomalous scattering).

atoms.title: NMR & the NOE distance ruler
atoms.summary: Nuclear spins report their chemical environment through chemical shift, and through cross-relaxation (the NOE) report inter-proton distances — structure in solution.

depths.eli5: Atomic nuclei act like tiny magnets. In a strong magnet they 'sing' at frequencies that depend on their neighbours, and nearby nuclei influence each other in a way that reveals how close they are.
depths.core: Each nucleus resonates at a frequency shifted by its local electronic environment — the chemical shift — fingerprinting chemical groups. The nuclear Overhauser effect (NOE) is dipolar cross-relaxation between nearby spins; its intensity scales steeply as r⁻⁶, so it is detectable only for protons within ~5 Å. A network of NOE-derived distance restraints, plus dihedral restraints from J-couplings, is fed to restrained dynamics to compute a structure.
depths.deep: Because NMR is done in solution at room temperature, the output is an ensemble of models consistent with the restraints, not a single static structure — it natively captures flexibility and exchange. Relaxation rates (T₁, T₂, ¹⁵N-NOE) report ps–ns backbone dynamics; relaxation dispersion probes µs–ms conformational exchange. Size is the limit: slow tumbling broadens lines, so beyond ~30–50 kDa you need TROSY, deuteration, and selective labeling.

atoms.note: NMR's r⁻⁶ NOE makes it a short-range ruler (only neighbors within ~5 Å); its solution-state answer is an ensemble of models, complementary to a crystal's single averaged structure. ('NMR' = nuclear magnetic resonance, the same physics as a hospital MRI; an ångström, Å, is a tenth of a nanometer, about the size of an atom.)

atoms.title: FRET — the spectroscopic ruler
atoms.summary: Energy hops non-radiatively from an excited donor dye to a nearby acceptor with an efficiency that falls as r⁻⁶ — a molecular tape measure for 2–10 nm.

depths.eli5: Attach two differently-coloured tags to a molecule. When they are close, one tag silently passes its energy to the other; how much it passes tells you how far apart they are.
depths.core: Förster resonance energy transfer is dipole–dipole coupling between a donor and acceptor whose emission and absorption spectra overlap. The transfer efficiency is E = 1/(1+(r/R₀)⁶), where R₀ (the Förster radius, typically 2–6 nm) is the distance giving 50% transfer. The steep r⁻⁶ dependence makes E exquisitely sensitive near R₀ — ideal for resolving conformational changes and binding.
depths.deep: R₀⁶ ∝ κ²·J·Q_D·n⁻⁴, where J is the spectral overlap, Q_D the donor quantum yield, n the refractive index, and κ² the orientation factor (often assumed 2/3 — a real source of error if the dyes are constrained). Single-molecule FRET (smFRET) resolves subpopulations and dwell times hidden in ensemble averages, mapping folding intermediates, motor stepping, and IDP conformational ensembles in real time.

atoms.note: The orientation factor κ² (usually assumed 2/3) is FRET's hidden uncertainty; the steep r⁻⁶ law makes it a precise ruler only near R₀. ('Donor' and 'acceptor' are two fluorescent dye tags; the donor is excited by light and can silently hand its energy to a nearby acceptor.)
atoms.art_prompt: an excited donor dye passing energy across a few nanometers to an acceptor dye, an efficiency curve falling sharply as r exceeds R-zero

quiz.prompt: Write the FRET efficiency as a function of distance and define R₀.
quiz.answer: E = 1/(1+(r/R₀)⁶). R₀, the Förster radius, is the donor–acceptor separation at which transfer efficiency is 50% (typically 2–6 nm).

quiz.prompt: Why is FRET most sensitive to distance changes near R₀, and what does smFRET add over ensemble FRET?
quiz.answer: The r⁻⁶ dependence makes dE/dr steepest around r = R₀, so small distance changes there cause large efficiency changes. Single-molecule FRET resolves subpopulations, intermediates, and dwell times that ensemble averaging washes out.

atoms.title: Cryo-EM & the contrast transfer function
atoms.summary: Flash-freeze molecules in vitreous ice, image thousands of noisy single particles, and reconstruct a 3D map — after correcting the microscope's oscillating contrast transfer function.

depths.eli5: Freeze molecules so fast the water turns glassy, take many blurry pictures of single particles in random orientations, and computationally combine them into a sharp 3D shape.
depths.core: Single-particle cryo-EM images many copies of a molecule frozen in random orientations in vitreous ice. Each image is extremely noisy and is modulated by the contrast transfer function — the microscope's point-spread in Fourier space, CTF(s) ≈ −sin(π·λ·Δz·s² − ½π·C_s·λ³·s⁴), which oscillates and zeroes out information at certain spatial frequencies. Estimating Δz (defocus) per micrograph and correcting the CTF is mandatory before averaging and 3D reconstruction.
depths.deep: Because the CTF flips sign and crosses zero, single defocus values leave gaps; collecting a range of defoci fills them. Resolution is reported via Fourier shell correlation (the FSC = 0.143 criterion). Unlike crystallography there is no crystal and no phase problem — phases come directly from the images — so flexible and heterogeneous complexes are tractable; 3D classification even resolves multiple conformational states from one dataset, making cryo-EM a structure *and* dynamics tool.

atoms.note: No crystal, no phase problem: cryo-EM gets the phases straight from the images, so flexible, varied assemblies that won't crystallize become solvable. ('Vitreous ice' is water frozen so fast it stays glassy instead of forming damaging crystals; 'defocus' is how far the microscope is from perfect focus.)

quiz.answer: The CTF is the microscope's transfer in Fourier space; it oscillates and crosses zero, flipping the sign of contrast and erasing information at certain spatial frequencies. It must be estimated (defocus) per image and corrected before averaging, or the reconstruction is wrong.

quiz.answer: No crystal is required and there is no phase problem (phases come from the images), so flexible, heterogeneous, or hard-to-crystallize complexes can be solved — and 3D classification can resolve multiple conformational states from a single dataset.

atoms.title: Helfrich membrane bending energy
atoms.summary: A fluid lipid bilayer behaves as a 2D elastic sheet whose energy cost is quadratic in curvature, governed by a bending modulus κ — the elasticity that sets the shapes of vesicles, tubes, and organelles.

depths.eli5: A soap-film-like membrane doesn't like to bend. The more sharply you curve it, the more energy it costs — and that simple rule explains why cells make round blobs, thin tubes, and folded shapes.
depths.core: Helfrich modeled the bilayer as a thin fluid elastic sheet. The bending energy per area is ½κ(2H − c₀)² + κ̄·K, where H is the mean curvature, K the Gaussian curvature, c₀ the spontaneous curvature, κ the bending modulus (~10–40 k_BT for lipids), and κ̄ the Gaussian (saddle-splay) modulus. Integrating over the surface gives the total cost of any shape; the equilibrium shape minimizes it (subject to area and volume constraints).
depths.deep: Because κ is only tens of k_BT, thermal fluctuations ripple the membrane — its fluctuation spectrum ⟨|h_q|²⟩ = k_BT/(κq⁴ + σq²) lets you read κ and tension σ from flicker microscopy. The Gaussian term integrates (Gauss–Bonnet) to a topological constant unless topology changes, so it only matters for fission/fusion. Spontaneous curvature c₀ from lipid shape or protein scaffolds (BAR domains) drives tubulation and budding — the physics behind endocytosis and organelle morphology.

atoms.note: κ (the bending stiffness) being only tens of k_BT means membranes are soft enough to ripple from heat yet stiff enough to hold a shape — the sweet spot biology exploits to remodel them. ('Curvature' measures how sharply a surface bends; 'mean curvature' is the average bend, 'Gaussian curvature' captures saddle-vs-dome shape.)

atoms.title: Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz voltage equation
atoms.summary: Generalizes the Nernst potential to a membrane permeable to several ions at once: the resting potential is a permeability-weighted blend of each ion's equilibrium potential.

depths.eli5: A cell's voltage isn't set by one ion but by a tug-of-war among several. Whichever ion the membrane lets through most easily pulls the voltage toward its own preferred value.
depths.core: When a membrane passes K⁺, Na⁺, and Cl⁻ simultaneously, the steady-state (zero net current) voltage is V_m = (RT/F)·ln[(P_K[K]_o + P_Na[Na]_o + P_Cl[Cl]_i)/(P_K[K]_i + P_Na[Na]_i + P_Cl[Cl]_o)]. Each permeability P weights that ion's contribution; anions appear with inside/outside flipped. At rest P_K dominates, so V_m sits near E_K but is pulled positive by the small Na⁺ leak.
depths.deep: GHK assumes a constant electric field across the membrane (the Goldman 'constant-field' approximation) and independent ion movement, yielding the GHK current equation whose zero-sum gives the voltage form. It explains why opening Na⁺ channels (raising P_Na) swings V_m toward E_Na during an action potential, and why the resting potential is never exactly any single Nernst potential — it is a dynamic, permeability-weighted compromise that channels actively retune.

atoms.note: Nernst is the single-ion equilibrium; GHK is the many-ion steady state (a balance with ions still flowing, but net zero current). Changing a 'permeability' — i.e. opening or closing a channel ('gating') — is how excitable cells slide their membrane voltage between the ions' Nernst potentials. ('Permeability' = how easily the membrane lets a given ion through.)

quiz.answer: The membrane potential when several ion species are permeant at once — a permeability-weighted combination of their equilibrium potentials, rather than the equilibrium potential of a single ion.

atoms.title: The cable equation
atoms.summary: Treats a dendrite or axon as a leaky electrical cable: voltage spreads passively with a characteristic length and time constant, setting how far and how fast signals travel before active channels regenerate them.

depths.eli5: A nerve fiber is like a leaky garden hose for voltage. Push voltage in at one spot and it spreads out, fading with distance and lagging in time — unless channels actively boost it along the way.
depths.core: Modeling the membrane as a resistive–capacitive cable gives ∂V/∂t = (λ²)·∂²V/∂x² − V (in units of the time constant τ), with space constant λ = √(r_m/r_i) and time constant τ = r_m·c_m. λ sets how far a passive signal decays to 1/e (∝ √diameter); τ sets how fast the membrane charges. Large λ and small τ mean fast, far-reaching passive spread.
depths.deep: The cable equation is the passive skeleton; Hodgkin–Huxley channels are the active flesh that turn decaying spread into a self-regenerating action potential. Conduction velocity scales with λ/τ, so thicker axons and — crucially — myelin (which raises r_m and lowers c_m) speed conduction; saltatory conduction jumps between nodes of Ranvier where the cable is actively re-excited. Dendritic cable theory (Rall) explains how synaptic inputs at different distances are filtered and summed at the soma.

atoms.note: λ (the space constant) and τ (the time constant) are the two numbers deciding whether a signal at a dendrite reaches the cell body (soma) in time to matter — the passive physics beneath neural computation. ('Dendrite' = the branch that receives inputs; 'axon' = the wire that sends the output; 'myelin' = a fatty insulating wrap that speeds conduction.)

atoms.title: Metropolis Monte Carlo sampling
atoms.summary: A stochastic algorithm that samples configurations with their Boltzmann probabilities by accepting or rejecting random moves — computing equilibrium averages without ever solving the dynamics.

depths.eli5: Instead of following a molecule's real motion, you propose random nudges and keep the ones that lower the energy (and sometimes the ones that raise it, by chance). Do this long enough and you visit shapes as often as nature would.
depths.core: Metropolis Monte Carlo generates a Markov chain over configurations. Propose a random move; if it lowers the energy (ΔE ≤ 0) accept it; if it raises the energy accept it with probability e^(−ΔE/k_BT), else reject and keep the current state. This acceptance rule satisfies detailed balance with the Boltzmann distribution, so the chain's stationary distribution is ∝ e^(−E/k_BT). Time averages over the chain converge to canonical ensemble averages.
depths.deep: MC needs no forces or time integration — only an energy function and a move set — so it can take large, unphysical jumps that cross barriers molecular dynamics would take ages to climb, but it gives no real kinetics (chain steps aren't time). Cleverness lives in move design (cluster moves, configurational-bias for polymers) and in beating critical slowing-down. Detailed balance, P(a)·W(a→b) = P(b)·W(b→a), is the load-bearing condition; break it carelessly and you sample the wrong distribution.

atoms.note: Monte Carlo trades real dynamics for sampling freedom: it reaches equilibrium averages efficiently but tells you nothing about speeds/rates — the complementary tradeoff to molecular dynamics. ('Markov chain' = a sequence of states where the next one depends only on the current one; 'detailed balance' is the symmetry condition that makes the chain settle to the right distribution.)

atoms.title: Free-energy methods: FEP, umbrella sampling & WHAM
atoms.summary: Simulation techniques that compute free-energy differences — the quantities that govern binding and folding — by reweighting biased or alchemically-perturbed ensembles rather than waiting for spontaneous transitions.

depths.eli5: Free energy is what decides which state wins, but the interesting states are rarely visited in a plain simulation. These methods gently push the system through the rare regions, then mathematically subtract the push back out.
depths.core: Free-energy perturbation uses ΔF = −k_BT·ln⟨e^(−(E_B−E_A)/k_BT)⟩_A to get the free-energy change for an alchemical transformation A→B from fluctuations sampled in state A. Umbrella sampling adds a biasing potential along a reaction coordinate to force sampling of high-energy regions in overlapping windows; WHAM (the weighted histogram analysis method) then optimally stitches the windows' biased histograms back into the unbiased potential of mean force.
depths.deep: The art is overlap: FEP's exponential average is dominated by rare low-energy tails, so A and B must have overlapping phase space (hence stratification into many small λ-windows, or Bennett acceptance ratio / MBAR which use both endpoints). Umbrella windows must overlap for WHAM to bridge them. These give the equilibrium PMF — the free-energy landscape — but not rates directly; combined with Kramers or transition-state ideas, the PMF's barrier height feeds a kinetic estimate. This is how computed binding affinities (ΔΔG of mutations, drug candidates) are made.

atoms.note: FEP and umbrella sampling + WHAM compute the free-energy landscape (ΔG, the 'potential of mean force') that plain MD visits too rarely to map — the bridge from simulation to measurable binding and folding free energies. ('Alchemical' = a non-physical computational trick that gradually morphs one molecule into another; a 'reaction coordinate' is a chosen progress axis from start to finish.)

quiz.answer: The exponential average is dominated by rare configurations where ΔE is very negative — the low-energy tail of B sampled from A. If A and B barely overlap, those configurations are essentially never sampled, so the average is unconverged and biased; this is why the transformation is split into many small, overlapping windows.

atoms.title: Markov state models
atoms.summary: Coarse-grains long or many short simulations into a network of metastable states with transition probabilities, recovering slow kinetics and rare-event rates that no single trajectory could reach.

depths.eli5: Chop a molecule's wiggling into a handful of 'rooms' and count how often it hops between them. The hopping statistics let you predict slow rearrangements you never watched happen in one go.
depths.core: An MSM partitions configuration space into discrete states and estimates a transition probability matrix T(τ) — the chance of moving between states in a lag time τ. If τ is long enough that jumps are memoryless (Markovian), the dynamics are fully captured by T. Its eigenvalues give relaxation timescales t_i = −τ/ln(λ_i); the slowest non-trivial eigenvectors identify the metastable states and the slow conformational processes.
depths.deep: The power move: stitch thousands of short, cheap, parallel trajectories into one global model of slow kinetics — you never need a single trajectory that crosses the barrier. Validity hinges on the Markov assumption, tested by the implied-timescales plot (timescales must plateau as τ grows) and the Chapman–Kolmogorov test. State definition matters: poor clustering breaks Markovianity, so modern pipelines learn collective variables (TICA, VAMPnets) before clustering. MSMs turn MD's sampling problem into a statistics problem and yield rates comparable to experiment.

atoms.note: MSMs recover slow rates from many short simulations by assuming memoryless hops between 'metastable' states (states the molecule lingers in for a while) — making rare events statistically reachable without ever simulating one end-to-end. ('Memoryless' / Markov = the next jump depends only on where you are now, not how you got there.)

atoms.title: Contact order & folding rate
atoms.summary: An empirical structural predictor of folding speed: proteins whose contacts are mostly between residues far apart in sequence fold more slowly than those stabilized by local contacts.

depths.eli5: If a protein is held together mostly by neighbors that sit close along the chain, it snaps shut fast. If it relies on partners at opposite ends of the chain finding each other, folding is slow.
depths.core: Relative contact order is CO = (1/(L·N))·Σ ΔS_ij, averaging the sequence separation ΔS_ij over all N native residue contacts in a chain of length L. Plaxco, Simons, and Baker found that for small two-state proteins, ln(k_f) of the folding rate correlates strongly (negatively) with relative contact order — high contact order means slow folding — often more predictively than thermodynamic stability does.
depths.deep: The result says topology, not just stability, sets folding kinetics: forming non-local contacts requires bringing distant chain segments together, paying a larger entropy cost in the transition state, which raises the folding barrier (linking to the two-state ΔG‡ picture). It rationalizes why all-α and local-β proteins fold fast while complex β-sheet topologies fold slowly, and it constrains funnel models — the transition-state ensemble's structure is encoded in which contacts must form. Variants (absolute CO, long-range order) refine the correlation across larger sets.

atoms.note: Contact order shows folding speed is a property of the native shape's 'topology' (the layout of which parts touch which), not just stability — contacts between residues far apart in the chain cost more entropy to form in the transition state, raising the folding barrier. ('Topology' here = the pattern of contacts; 'two-state' folder = one that's either fully folded or fully unfolded.)
